title: The smaller footprint
hook: a good tracker doesn't conclude from a small footprint; the gradual training

segments.voice: Yesterday: ariyapariyesana, a being who ages looking for what doesn't. Did you pause before one search and ask what you were really looking for? Day four hundred twenty-five.

A wanderer named Pilotika is walking back from a visit to the Buddha, full of admiration. The brahmin Janussoni stops him and asks why he's so sure the Buddha is the real thing. Pilotika says: I'm like an elephant tracker who sees a huge footprint and knows, that's a great bull elephant. I've seen four footprints of this man, and I'm sure. The brahmin carries the story to the Buddha. And the Buddha, of all people, says: not so fast. Today: the smaller footprint.
screen: `PILOTIKA IS SURE.` → `FOUR FOOTPRINTS, ONE GREAT ELEPHANT.` → `THE BUDDHA: NOT SO FAST.`

segments.voice: This is the twenty-seventh discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the shorter discourse on the simile of the elephant's footprint. The Buddha finishes Pilotika's picture properly. A skilled tracker enters an elephant forest and sees a big footprint, long and broad. He doesn't conclude. There are female dwarf elephants with big feet. Then he sees a big footprint, and high marks where the bark is scraped. Still he doesn't conclude. Tall female elephants could make those. Then tusk marks high on the trees. Still not: tall females with tusks could make those. Only when he sees broken branches too, and then the bull elephant itself, under a tree or in the open, does he say: this is the great one. Then the Buddha lays out the gradual training. Someone hears the teaching, gains trust, and goes forth. They keep the precepts. They guard the senses, stay mindful in everything they do, and find a quiet place to sit. The hindrances fall away. They enter the first absorption, then the second, the third, the fourth. Each of these, the Buddha says, is a footprint. But a noble disciple doesn't conclude yet. Then come deep knowledges, and still not. Only at the end, when the mind is freed and they know it's freed, do they say: the teacher is truly awakened, and the teaching is well proclaimed. It's a caution aimed at praise of the teacher himself. A good feeling in meditation is a footprint, not the elephant. A good first week at anything is a footprint. Keep tracking.
screen: `PILOTIKA'S PRAISE, AND A CORRECTION` · `A BIG PRINT COULD BE A SMALLER ELEPHANT` · `THE GRADUAL TRAINING, STEP BY STEP` · `ONLY THE ELEPHANT ITSELF SETTLES IT` · then, large: `NOT YET THE ELEPHANT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Within a few breaths, the mind will offer a verdict: this is going well, or this isn't working, or I'm bad at this. Notice the verdict. Call it a footprint. Then keep sitting, and see what comes next. If another verdict arrives, call that a footprint too. You're tracking, not deciding. The bell holds the time.
hatthipada. A big print that might belong to a smaller animal: a sign worth following, not yet a reason to conclude. Today's word.
Your line: not yet the elephant. Today, when you catch yourself deciding about a person or a situation from one sign, say the line, and wait for more tracks. Day four hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Theravada teachers present MN 27 as a model of the gradual training, from hearing the teaching and keeping precepts to meditation and liberation, and use the tracker's patience to caution students against mistaking early meditative experiences for the goal.

pairs: could be a female dwarf elephant

myth: the Buddha accepted Pilotika's praise as it stood
he said the simile wasn't complete yet, and finished it properly.
in MN 27 even the four absorptions are only footprints
a noble disciple doesn't conclude from them; only liberation settles it.
a skilled tracker concludes from the biggest print
big prints can belong to smaller elephants; he waits to see the bull itself.

fork.setup: you're a tracker. you find a long, broad footprint and high scrape marks on the trees. what do you conclude?
options: a great bull elephant, for sure.
nothing yet: tall females can leave these too.
fork.reveal: the Buddha's tracker keeps going past every sign until he sees the bull elephant itself, in a clearing or under a tree.

original.note: Pali hatthipada: elephant's footprint. hatthi (elephant) + pada (foot, footprint).

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about being careful in the forest.
what it means: every good sign along the path is a footprint, worth following, not yet the goal.

what a scholar hears: MN 27 is a classic statement of the gradual training (anupubba sikkha), a sequence that recurs in other discourses such as DN 2, from going forth through the jhanas to the destruction of the taints.
recall: a lion's roar: a bold claim

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 27, Culahatthipadopama Sutta (the shorter simile of the elephant's footprint)

notes: MN 27 paraphrased: the brahmin is Janussoni; the tracker's sequence (dwarf she-elephants, tall she-elephants, scrapes, tusk marks) abridged. Confirm.
The gradual training summarized briefly; 'deep knowledges' stands for recollection of past lives and the divine eye.
Devanagari hatthipada and the term anupubba sikkha in the trapdoor: confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): tracker sequence corrected (tusk marks with tall tusked females; broken branches only with the final sighting); Pilotika was returning from the Buddha, not 'out of the forest', and the brahmin is now named (Janussoni); cut 'eat in moderation' (not in MN 27's list) and the garbled 'his own followers' praise' line.
